stories.headline: Update: Russia Launches Massive Drone and Missile Barrage on Kyiv, Killing at Least 16
stories.summary:
Russia launched one of its largest attacks of the war against Ukraine overnight Thursday into Friday, firing more than 670 drones and 56 missiles at Kyiv and other regions, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. At least 16 people were killed, including two children, when a nine-story apartment building in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district was partially destroyed. Rescuers are still searching for at least 20 people feared missing, and 47 others were injured. Friday was declared a day of mourning in Kyiv.

The strikes hit more than 180 sites across Ukraine, including more than 50 residential buildings. Ukraine reported an overall drone interception rate of 93%, but only 73% for missiles, with Zelensky identifying Russian ballistic missiles as the key remaining defensive challenge. He called the assault "definitely not the actions of those who believe the war is coming to an end" and urged allies to accelerate deliveries of anti-ballistic systems, including U.S.-made Patriot batteries.

The attack is the third consecutive day Ukraine has reported fatalities, following the expiration of a brief ceasefire on Monday. Since Tuesday night, more than 1,560 Russian drones have targeted Ukrainian cities, Zelensky said. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned Moscow for "indiscriminately targeting civilians" and announced the bloc is finalizing a €6 billion drone support package for Ukraine.

The scale of the strike represents a significant escalation in Russian offensive tempo. Ukraine has repeatedly warned it faces a critical shortage of air defense munitions. The attacks come as diplomatic efforts involving the U.S., Europe, and Russia remain stalled, with no ceasefire negotiations scheduled.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says He Made No Commitment on Taiwan After Xi Issues Stark Warning at Beijing Summit
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump concluded his two-day summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing on Friday, departing with no major trade deals announced and unresolved differences on Taiwan, Iran, and other core flashpoints. Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One, Trump said he "made no commitment either way" on Taiwan, adding he would decide soon on a delayed $14 billion U.S. arms sale to the island. Xi had issued an unusually direct warning during talks that tensions over Taiwan could lead to "clashes and even conflicts" between the world's two largest economies.

The summit produced choreographed pageantry — including a rare private tour of the Zhongnanhai leadership compound — but no substantive breakthroughs. Trump claimed Xi pledged not to supply Iran with military equipment, calling it a major win, and said the two leaders agreed the Strait of Hormuz should remain open to global shipping. China's foreign ministry said it saw "no point" in the continuation of the U.S.-Iran conflict, though U.S. officials acknowledged Beijing had not committed to actively pressuring Tehran.

On trade, Trump suggested Boeing had secured an order for approximately 200 aircraft from Chinese carriers, though details on numbers and timing remained vague. Trump also said he did not ask Xi for "any favors" on Iran, explaining that requesting favors requires giving favors in return. No extension of the existing tariff truce was announced, and soybean and corn futures fell after traders found little new substance in the summit's outcome.

Analysts described the results as a modest stabilization rather than a reset. Xi declared the visit a "historic" landmark, while U.S. observers noted that nearly every structural tension in the bilateral relationship — trade, Taiwan, Iran, artificial intelligence — remained unresolved. The summit is the first U.S. presidential visit to China in nearly a decade.

stories.headline: U.S. Plans to Indict Former Cuban President Raúl Castro, DOJ Official Says
stories.summary:
The United States is preparing criminal charges against former Cuban President Raúl Castro, 94, a Justice Department official told Reuters on Friday, describing the potential indictment as imminent. The charges are expected to center on Cuba's 1996 downing of two small planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a Cuban-American humanitarian group, which killed four U.S. citizens. The indictment must still be approved by a grand jury, and its precise timing was not immediately clear.

The announcement comes one day after CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Havana to meet with top Cuban officials, including Raulito Rodriguez Castro, Raúl Castro's grandson. That meeting, the highest-level U.S. intelligence visit to Cuba in recent memory, focused on intelligence cooperation and security issues. A CIA official said Ratcliffe emphasized that cooperation was possible if Cuba made "fundamental changes," while also warning that the window for negotiations was not indefinite.

The planned indictment represents a significant escalation of U.S. pressure on the Cuban government, which is simultaneously facing a severe domestic energy and economic crisis. Trump has publicly mused about regime change in Cuba, and the administration has renewed a $100 million aid offer conditioned on political reforms. The juxtaposition of diplomatic outreach and criminal charges reflects the administration's dual-track strategy toward Havana.

The 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown has long been a grievance for Cuban-American communities and a legal pressure point against Havana. Filing charges against a former head of state would be an extraordinary legal and diplomatic step with few modern precedents, and the move is expected to draw strong condemnation from Cuba and its allies.

stories.headline: Update: New Forecasts Warn of Record Global Temperatures as 'Super El Niño' Strengthens
stories.summary:
New forecasts from NOAA, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and Australia's Bureau of Meteorology are converging on a high-confidence assessment that a potentially historic El Niño is developing in the tropical Pacific. NOAA now places a two-in-three probability that the pattern will be strong or very strong by winter, with some models projecting sea surface temperatures in the key Niño3.4 monitoring region could exceed 2.5°C above normal — a threshold scientists describe as a "historically strong event." A small subset of forecast models suggests temperatures could surpass 3°C, which would exceed the previous known record set in 1877.

The rate of warming seen in the tropical Pacific over recent weeks is itself notable: NOAA meteorologist Nathanial Johnson described the pace — moving from a La Niña pattern in winter to a potentially strong El Niño within a single year — as a "rare occurrence." Scientists warn the event, if it peaks as projected in autumn, would likely make 2027 the warmest year on record globally, with cascading effects on weather patterns including droughts across parts of Asia, Africa, and South America.

The 1877 El Niño, the historical benchmark some models now approach, lasted approximately 18 months and triggered catastrophic drought and famine across multiple continents. Modern forecasting tools and earlier warning allow for more preparation, but humanitarian agencies and governments in vulnerable regions will need to begin contingency planning now, scientists said.

While spring El Niño forecasts have historically carried significant uncertainty, experts noted that confidence this year is unusually high across multiple independent modeling centers — a convergence that itself is scientifically significant. NOAA said El Niño onset is expected within the current month.

stories.headline: Update: Trump-Xi Summit Ends With Stabilized Relations but No Formal Breakthroughs
stories.summary:
President Trump departed Beijing on Thursday after two days of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, concluding what both sides described as a historic summit but one that produced no formal agreements on the major issues dividing the two powers. Trump said "a lot of different problems" were settled, though substantive announcements on trade, Iran, or Taiwan have yet to materialize. The summit is the highest-level U.S.-China engagement in years, occurring against a backdrop of ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict and severe global economic disruption from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

On Iran, the two leaders agreed Tehran should not possess nuclear weapons, and a potential U.S.-China energy deal — under which Beijing would purchase more American energy in lieu of Iranian oil — was reported to be in early discussions. However, Beijing largely reiterated its existing position, and analysts said the summit moved the needle little on ending the conflict. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, speaking in New Delhi, welcomed any Chinese diplomatic effort and said Tehran was open to Beijing's mediation.

On Taiwan, Xi told Trump the island was "the most important issue" in U.S.-China relations and delivered an explicit warning. Secretary of State Marco Rubio responded by saying U.S. policy on Taiwan is "unchanged," appearing to quell fears that Trump might use Taiwan as a bargaining chip in broader negotiations. On trade, Trump returned with what he called economic wins, though no formal agreements were confirmed by either government.

The summit leaves the bilateral relationship in a more stable but unresolved state. Supporters of the engagement argue that direct leader-level contact reduces the risk of miscalculation during a period of global crisis; critics caution that a cordial atmosphere without binding commitments may give Beijing leverage without requiring concessions. The meeting was covered by more than two dozen major outlets, reflecting its status as one of the most consequential diplomatic events of the year.

stories.headline: Ebola Outbreak Declared in Eastern DR Congo; 65 Dead, 246 Cases Reported
stories.summary:
Africa's top health agency declared an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo's eastern Ituri province on Friday, with approximately 246 cases and 65 deaths reported, concentrated in the gold-mining towns of Mongwalu and Rwampara. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said it was convening an emergency meeting with DRC, neighboring Uganda, South Sudan, and international partners to coordinate response efforts and cross-border surveillance. The Congolese government had not yet officially declared an outbreak as of Friday, though a press conference was expected.

Preliminary laboratory tests at the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in Kinshasa detected the Ebola virus in 13 of 20 analyzed samples. Africa CDC expressed concern about the high risk of further spread due to the urban settings of the affected towns, ongoing mining activity driving population movement, and proximity to international borders. Additional suspected cases have been reported in Ituri's provincial capital, Bunia, with laboratory confirmation pending.

Ebola, first identified in 1976 in what is now DRC, spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids and carries an average fatality rate of roughly 50 percent, according to the World Health Organization. This is the country's 17th outbreak of the disease. The deadliest DRC outbreak, between 2018 and 2020, killed nearly 2,300 people; a separate outbreak in central Kasai province last year killed 45.

Ituri province has been under military rule since 2021 due to ongoing armed group activity, including forces affiliated with the Islamic State group, complicating the public health response. Africa CDC executive director Dr. Jean Kaseya warned that "significant population movement" between affected areas and neighboring countries makes regional coordination essential.

stories.headline: Update: UK's Starmer Faces Open Party Rebellion as Health Secretary Quits and Rivals Position for Challenge
stories.summary:
British Health Secretary Wes Streeting resigned from Prime Minister Keir Starmer's Cabinet on Thursday, becoming the first senior minister to publicly break with the government and positioning himself as a likely leadership challenger. In a sharply worded resignation letter, Streeting said he had "lost confidence" in Starmer, writing: "Where we need vision, we have a vacuum. Where we need direction, we have drift." He called on Starmer to step aside to allow a broad field of candidates to contest the party's future direction, though he stopped short of explicitly declaring his own candidacy.

The resignation follows devastating results for Labour in last week's local and regional elections, which hardened doubts within the party about Starmer's political judgment and long-term viability as a leader. Two other senior figures — Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner and Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham — are also reportedly positioning themselves for potential leadership bids. Starmer responded to Streeting's departure with a conciliatory letter, saying he was "truly sorry" to see him leave and making no direct reference to his criticisms.

This is a material escalation of the previously covered leadership crisis: Streeting's formal resignation from Cabinet represents the rebellion moving from speculation to concrete action, crossing a significant threshold. The Starmer government, which returned Labour to power in July 2024 after 14 years in opposition, is now facing a genuine internal insurgency less than two years into its term. Streeting praised Starmer for "keeping Britain out of the war in Iran" but argued that domestic leadership had been inadequate.

The political situation remains fluid. No formal leadership challenge has been triggered, and Starmer has indicated he intends to continue governing. Whether Streeting's departure prompts a cascade of further resignations or a formal confidence vote will determine the near-term survival of the government.

stories.headline: Update: CDC Monitoring 41 People in U.S. for Hantavirus; No Confirmed American Cases
stories.summary:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Thursday it is monitoring 41 people in the United States for possible Andes hantavirus infection, up from previous figures, but confirmed there are no cases of the disease on American soil. Eighteen of the individuals under monitoring are quarantined in Nebraska and Atlanta. CDC incident manager David Fitter told reporters the agency does not plan to impose movement restrictions on those being tracked, and most have been advised to remain at home and limit contact with others.

The monitoring program stems from the outbreak that killed three people aboard a luxury cruise ship earlier this month. The Andes strain of hantavirus, which can spread person-to-person unlike other hantavirus variants, has been at the center of international concern since cases emerged among cruise ship passengers. Previously covered developments included a French patient placed on an artificial lung, contact cases isolating on remote Pitcairn Islands, and WHO stating it saw no sign of a larger outbreak.

The updated figure of 41 people under surveillance represents a concrete new data point in an evolving public health situation. Hantavirus causes severe respiratory illness and carries a significant fatality rate; the Andes variant's capacity for human-to-human transmission makes it of particular concern to health authorities. The CDC's decision not to impose movement restrictions suggests officials currently assess the risk of broader community spread in the United States as low.

Health authorities continue to conduct contact tracing and laboratory testing on individuals who may have been exposed through the cruise ship. No timeline has been given for when those under monitoring will be cleared.
